After collecting a half-dozen females of this newly recorded species for New Hampshire, I finally got a male! I had placed my supercharged dung beetle trap about 30 ft. from a giant pile of cow dung being composted in a field. This male and four females, plus several O. hecate and two O. nuchicornis showed up on the second day of trap operation. It was a very warm day and had been warm overnight as well. I was eager to collect and photograph a male because of its sensational headgear -- the back-swooping horns from which it gets its name. The species is native to Europe and the Middle East, and has spread rapidly since being introduced in the southern US. This individual will be donated to the University of New Hampshire insect collection, Donald Chandler, curator. lifeStage:adult Sex:male Size:9.5 - 10.5 mm

It has horns resembling Onthophagus gaz*ella's but it is a minor male of Onthophagus taurus. Apparently some minor males have only a hint of horn buds. Minor males tend to be smaller and have shorter wings than major males. A hormonal switch that triggers large horns when the pronotum reaches a certain width fails to activate if the larval food supply is inadequate to make a wide pronotum. The short-horned males then try to sneak copulation with receptive females while major males scuffle with their large horns. lifeStage:adult Sex:male Size:9 mm
